story: Inuit knew these mountains as Torngait, the place of spirits, home of Torngarsoak, the most powerful of them, who controlled the animals of the sea and took the form of a huge polar bear. Inuit have lived, hunted and travelled here for centuries, and they still do, all year round, though nobody lives inside the park today. Parks Canada gives the park its Inuttitut name, Tongait KakKasuangita SilakKijapvinga, alongside the English one, and runs it with Inuit of Nunatsiavut in Labrador and Nunavik in Quebec. Inuit describe it as a place where they say Alianattuk: this is a good place to be.

The rocks span about eighty per cent of the Earth's history. Gneiss at Saglek Bay has been dated to 3.9 billion years, and only two places in the world have older rock; the 1.9-billion-year-old sedimentary rocks of the Ramah Group still carry their ripple marks. At least five episodes of mountain building, from the Archean to the opening of the Labrador Sea, are laid out in cliffs that cut across the grain of the rock. Ice carved the rest: U-shaped valleys, hanging valleys, horns and arêtes, and fjords such as Nachvak and Saglek where cliffs rise more than 900 metres from the sea. The peaks along the Quebec border are the highest in mainland Canada east of the Rockies, topped by Mount Caubvick at 1,652 metres, and more than 40 small glaciers cling to their cirques, the last in eastern continental North America.

The whole park lies north of the tree line. About 330 kinds of flowering plant and fern and 220 mosses and liverworts grow here, richest on raised beaches, in coastal meadows and along limestone streams, and berry shrubs feed bears in late summer. The small Torngat Mountains caribou herd ranges over much of the park, and George River caribou wander in after calving. Polar bears hunt seals along the ice and frequent the coast in summer; an unusual population of black bears lives out on the tundra, and wolves follow the caribou. Arctic hares and rock ptarmigan stay through the winter, while seals and whales move north along the coast each summer.

Hundreds of archaeological sites, some nearly 7,000 years old, record Maritime Archaic peoples, Pre-Dorset and Dorset Palaeo-Eskimos and the Thule culture from which today's Inuit descend: tent rings, stone caribou fences, food caches and graves. Chert from the Ramah quarries was traded as far south as Maine. Later came Moravian missions, Hudson's Bay Company posts in Saglek and Nachvak, a German automatic weather station landed by submarine in 1943 and two Cold War radar sites. After Newfoundland joined Canada in 1949, Inuit in the northern settlements were forcibly moved south. The park was created with the consent of Inuit: a park reserve in 2005 under the Labrador Inuit Land Claims Agreement, and a national park in 2008 under the Nunavik Inuit Land Claims Agreement.
howItWorks: Torngat Mountains National Park is remote wilderness with no roads, trails, signs or facilities, open all year but practical to visit only in summer and in late winter and early spring. The 2026 visitor season ran from mid-July to late August. Every visitor must register with Parks Canada before entering, attend a safety briefing and orientation that includes polar bear safety, and deregister on leaving; if you do not deregister, staff may start a search. Register through the park office in Nain, by phone on 1-888-922-1290, or at the Torngat Mountains Base Camp and Research Station. Parks Canada does not list Torngat among its Discovery Pass places and publishes no admission fee for it; ask the Nain office about any fees before you go.

Most visitors stay at the Torngat Mountains Base Camp and Research Station, just outside the park's southern boundary at Kangidluasuk (St. John's Harbour) in Saglek Bay. It is surrounded by an electric bear fence, and its packages include charter flights from Goose Bay to Saglek, boat or helicopter transfers, meals, tent accommodation and guided trips, with Parks Canada staff giving interpretation in the park and Inuit bear guards along. Experienced independent travellers are welcome but must be self-reliant: contact Parks Canada well in advance and submit an itinerary, a gear list and a safety plan that includes how you will avoid and handle bears.

Visitors may not carry firearms in the park; experienced Inuit polar bear guards are permitted to, and Parks Canada strongly recommends travelling with one. Aircraft may land only with a permit under exceptional circumstances, and snowmobiling is allowed only under special circumstances. Inuit continue to hunt, fish and travel throughout the park. Research permit applications for 2027 are due before 1 March 2027, and commercial guiding needs a commercial use permit from the Nain office.

sightNotes.poi-ca-torngat-mountains-saglek-fiord: The park's southern boundary and the usual way in. Gneiss around Saglek Bay is among the oldest dated rock on Earth, 3.9 billion years old.
sightNotes.poi-ca-torngat-mountains-silluak-north-a: A branch of Saglek Fiord between fjord walls about 900 metres high. Day trips from Base Camp land here to walk past old caches and hunting blinds to waterfalls and a sandy-beached lake.
sightNotes.poi-ca-torngat-mountains-pitukkik-nakvak: A traditional Inuit route from the Labrador coast to Ungava Bay, marked at its mouth by a commemorative inuksuk. The full trek runs about 68 kilometres over five or six days.
sightNotes.poi-ca-torngat-mountains-nachvak-fiord: A deep fjord in the heart of the range, its cliffs rising more than 900 metres straight from the water, with the site of an old Hudson's Bay Company post.
sightNotes.poi-ca-torngat-mountains-mount-caubvick: The highest peak in mainland Canada east of the Rockies, 1,652 metres, on the Quebec border, where it is called Mont D'Iberville. Small glaciers cling to the cirques around it.
sightNotes.poi-ca-torngat-mountains-ramah-bay: The remains of a Moravian mission where Inuit and Europeans lived side by side from 1871 to 1908, near the ancient kitjigattalik–Ramah chert quarries.

entrances: Torngat Mountains Base Camp and Research Station at Kangidluasuk (St. John's Harbour), Saglek Bay, outside the southern boundary — by charter flight from Goose Bay to Saglek, then boat or helicopter
Nain, on the Labrador coast — the Parks Canada office, and air or boat charters with Inuit guides
Kuujjuaq in Nunavik — air charters; Parks Canada also has an office in Kangiqsualujjuaq
On foot from Parc national Kuururjuaq in Quebec, along the Nakvak Brook route
planYourVisit.reservations: There is no Parks Canada booking for the park itself. Base Camp packages, flights and boat charters are booked with the operators, and every trip must be registered with Parks Canada beforehand. Check before you go.

chronology.text: The oldest of the park's hundreds of archaeological sites date from this time; Maritime Archaic peoples were the first to quarry Ramah chert.
The Moravian Church opens a mission at Ramah, where Inuit and Europeans live side by side until 1908.
A German submarine lands an automatic weather station on the Hutton Peninsula in October.
Newfoundland and Labrador joins Canada; Inuit in the smaller northern settlements are later forcibly moved south.
Torngat Mountains National Park Reserve is established with the Labrador Inuit Land Claims Agreement.
The park reserve becomes a national park under the Nunavik Inuit Land Claims Agreement.
A new management plan, Tongait KakKasuangita SilakKijapvinga, is approved.

safety: The chance of meeting a polar bear or black bear is extremely high. Travel with an experienced Inuit bear guard, carry deterrents such as crackers, screamers and air horns and know how to use them, and fence your camp at night.
Snow, low cloud and violent winds can arrive in any month, and temperatures can fall more than 10 °C within minutes. Carry clothing and food for long weather delays.
There are no trails. Navigate with 1:50,000 topographic maps, compass and GPS, and do not rely on route descriptions alone.
Carry a satellite phone; Iridium works best here. Parks Canada emergency dispatch is 1-780-852-3100, as the toll-free number may not work from satellite phones; the RCMP in Nain is 1-709-922-2862.
Filter, treat or boil all drinking water.
regulations: Register before entering, attend the safety briefing and orientation, and deregister when you leave.
Visitors may not carry firearms in the park; only permitted Inuit bear guards may.
Leave tent rings, graves, hunting blinds, fox traps, caches, cairns and inuksuit untouched, and do not build new ones; do not camp on archaeological sites.
Aircraft may land only with a permit, and food caches need Parks Canada's permission.
Never light fires on moss or tundra; pack out all litter.

weather: Altitude, latitude and the cold Labrador Sea make the climate harsh. On the mountains along the Quebec border, snow, low cloud and extremely high winds can come in any month, and sudden 'ghost winds' can sweep down from the peaks from any direction, strong enough to knock people over. Along the coast and fjords the Labrador Current brings cold air, fog, drizzle and days of low cloud, and icebergs drift past all summer. In the sheltered inland valleys a calm summer day can pass 20 °C, but wind off the snowfields can drop the temperature by more than 10 °C within minutes. The north of the park is cooler and foggier still. Plan for delays: weather can pin a party down for days.
directions: There are no roads. Base Camp's packages include air travel from Goose Bay to Saglek via Nain, then boat or helicopter to camp; PAL Airlines flies to Goose Bay daily from St. John's, Gander and Deer Lake, and on some days from Montreal and Halifax. Air charters also fly from Goose Bay and from Kuujjuaq in Nunavik, and boat charters with guides can be arranged from Nain; private boats may enter the park after registration. Parks Canada and the Nunatsiavut Government can put you in touch with local operators.
